 Panama Catholic Church reports dozens of clerical abuse cases 







PANAMA CITY, Panama (AFP) — The Catholic Church in Panama has recorded dozens of complaints alleging sexual abuse of minors and other vulnerable people by priests, according to a report released Tuesday.

Prepared by two Catholic universities at the request of the church, the report found 37 complaints for sexual abuse were filed against clergy members between 2001 and 2025.

The Archbishop of Panama City, Jose Domingo Ulloa, said in a presentation of the report that it sought to determine how the church had managed “this entire reality of sexual abuse against minors.”

He repeated an apology he made in 2023 to the victims and said five clergy members were defrocked after being convicted of sexual abuse.

Around the world, the Catholic Church has been tainted by scandals involving decades of child sexual abuse by pedophile priests.

The Panama report found no evidence of a deliberate policy of concealment of abuse by the church in the Central American country, but did flag problems in how the complaints were handled.

The report was compiled by Spain’s Villanueva University with the University of Notre Dame in the United States.

Maria Jose Valero, one of the authors, noted that the number of complaints made did not necessarily reflect the scale of the abuse, given the reluctance of some victims to come forward.

A 2019 report by the Child Rights International Network showed that while Latin America was the world’s most Catholic continent it had the lowest rates of reporting of clerical sexual abuse.

news.title: South Korea's Lee, Trump welcome progress in US strategic investment projects
news.text:
SEOUL: South Korean ‌President Lee Jae Myung and US President Donald Trump welcomed “significant progress” in discussions on strategic investment projects during a 30-minute meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Seoul’s presidential office said on Wednesday.

The meeting came after South Korea’s Industry Ministry briefed lawmakers on Tuesday ​on implementation plans under the countries’ $350 billion investment package, including a Texas gas-fired power project identified as a ​potential first investment, as well as possible investments in nuclear energy and an Alaska LNG ⁠project.

“The two leaders welcomed the significant progress made in discussions on strategic investment projects between the two countries,” ​National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac told a briefing.

Based on the joint statement issued after their summit last November, Lee and ​Trump also agreed to deepen cooperation and continue discussions on issues including nuclear fuel enrichment and reprocessing, nuclear-powered submarines, shipbuilding and the transfer of wartime operational control (OPCON) from the US to South Korea, Wi said.

Trump also reaffirmed his willingness to engage in dialogue with ​North Korea, Wi said, with the two leaders agreeing to remain in close communication in pursuit of a peace ​process.

Lee also said the US-China summit scheduled for Thursday would be important for regional developments, including South Korea-China relations, and expressed hope ‌for ⁠a successful meeting, according to Wi.

Earlier on Wednesday, Lee told the UN General Assembly that Seoul would support efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea and work toward a durable peace framework while seeking broader international backing for those efforts.

A senior presidential official separately told several South Korean media outlets that Lee had told Trump he hoped the US ​president would help advance engagement ​with North Korea, to ⁠which Trump replied that he would do so.

The official said Trump also remarked that he maintained a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, though there was ​no indication of any specific contact currently taking place, the media reports said.

The official ​also said Lee ⁠and Trump spent considerable time discussing OPCON transfer, with Trump gaining a better understanding of Seoul’s position. The US side stressed the need to meet the required conditions and complete the process as soon as possible, the reports said.

The official was ⁠also quoted ​as saying that progress in talks on South Korean investments in ​US projects helped pave the way for the summit, which had not initially been expected to take place.

Trump is expected to personally announce Seoul’s ​investment plans once an agreement is reached, South Korean media reported.

news.title: Indian rupee hooked to oil prices as markets gauge Iran diplomacy hopes
news.text:
MUMBAI: The Indian rupee is poised for a muted start on Wednesday and traders reckon that directional moves will be contingent on ​oil prices amid hopes of a diplomatic solution to the US-Iran ‌war through talks at the UN.

The Indian rupee is expected to open nearly flat around 95.60-95.65 per dollar compared to its close at 95.59 in the previous session.

Oil ​markets remain the key driver for Indian assets with Brent crude ​futures hovering near two-week lows at $99.22 per barrel, on hopes ⁠that diplomacy at the UN General Assembly could pave the way ​for a resolution to the Middle East war.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday ​said that he could annihilate Iran if there is no deal, but also suggested an agreement could come soon.

“For Asia in particular, the good news is that oil prices ​have moderated somewhat from the highs,” analysts at MUFG said in a note, ​while cautioning that “the path forward remains unclear given the lack of clarity around a possible ‌resolution ⁠of the conflict.”

Regional currencies traded mixed while shares across Asia were mostly higher, buoyed by signs of healthy consumer demand for AI apps. India has remained a laggard among regional equity markets due to its lack of AI-linked ​opportunities, contributing to ​weakness in foreign ⁠flows to its equity market.

Overseas traders have sold Indian shares worth $1.81 billion so far in September, taking year-to-date outflows to $25.87 billion, according ​to stock depository data.

Weakness in capital flows and stress ​on account of ⁠an elevated energy bill has translated to pressure on the rupee, partially absorbed by frequent central bank interventions, that have kept the currency’s losses in check.

Traders reckon that rhythm ⁠is likely ​to persist in the near-term, especially after ​the central bank’s bountiful haul of capital inflows under one-off policy measures to attract foreign currency boosted India’s ​FX reserves to a record high.

news.title: US Military Bases in Greenland: What the New Defense Deal Means
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta – The United States (US), Denmark and Greenland have signed a new defense agreement allowing Washington to establish two additional military facilities in Greenland while reaffirming Danish sovereignty over the strategically important Arctic territory.US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the agreement on Sept. 22 on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, as reported by BBC.Trump said the United States would immediately begin developing a larger military presence in Greenland, including two major military bases. The agreement expands Washington's existing military role on the island while formally recognizing Denmark's sovereignty and Greenland's right to self-determination.The deal amends and updates a 1951 defense agreement between the United States and Denmark. It still requires approval from both the Danish and Greenlandic parliaments.Where Will the US Build the New Military Bases?The agreement identifies Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and Mestersvig in eastern Greenland as locations for additional US defense areas, according to Al Jazeera.NarsarsuaqNarsarsuaq is a former US military base and civilian airport in southern Greenland. The United States operated the site during World War II and the Cold War before closing its military base there in 1958.The site has a large runway and access to deep water. US military engineers recently surveyed the area, according to US North Command, making it a suitable location for renewed military activity.The new agreement would effectively bring the former US military site back into Washington's defense network in Greenland.MestersvigMestersvig is a remote military outpost in eastern Greenland that is currently used by Denmark's Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a special forces unit responsible for patrolling the vast Arctic territory.Unlike Narsarsuaq, Mestersvig is relatively undeveloped and isolated. The agreement allows the United States to establish an additional defense area there, although the precise arrangements and technical details have yet to be finalized.The locations and operations of the new facilities must be mutually agreed upon by the United States, Denmark and Greenland.What Does the Agreement Mean for Greenland's Sovereignty?The agreement does not transfer Greenlandic territory to the United States.It explicitly recognizes Denmark's sovereignty and territorial integrity while also recognizing Greenland's right to self-determination. Greenland is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.The agreement also states that Greenland would remain part of NATO if it becomes independent in the future.For Greenland, the agreement marks a significant shift from the confrontation that began after Trump repeatedly called for greater US control of the territory.Nielsen described the deal as a "win-win-win" and said it takes into account Greenland's people, rights, livelihoods and development.Frederiksen likewise said the agreement respects both Danish sovereignty and Greenland's right to self-determination.How Will the Deal Expand US Military Presence?The United States already operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, where American personnel carry out missile warning and space-related missions.The new agreement allows Washington to modernize and expand its activities at Pituffik while establishing the additional defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig.The agreement also gives the United States broader military access, including rights related to aircraft operations and undersea access in Greenland.At the same time, the pact places restrictions on other countries. Non-NATO states will not be permitted to establish manned or unmanned military installations or maintain a persistent military presence in Greenland.The agreement also contains provisions designed to prevent sensitive investments by countries outside NATO and the European Union that could pose security concerns.Why Is Greenland Strategically Important?Greenland sits between North America and Europe and occupies a strategically important position in the Arctic and North Atlantic.Its location has long made the territory important to US and NATO defense planning. Greenland also possesses significant mineral resources, including rare-earth deposits, adding an economic dimension to the strategic competition surrounding the Arctic.Trump has repeatedly cited security concerns involving Russia and China when arguing that the United States needs a stronger position in Greenland.The new agreement specifically prevents non-NATO countries from establishing a military presence on the island, effectively limiting the ability of potential US rivals to develop their own bases there.Russia said it was not involved in negotiations over the agreement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said cooperation with Russia in the Arctic was currently not on the agenda, while China has not publicly commented on the deal.A Shift After Months of TensionThe agreement follows more than a year of tension after Trump repeatedly threatened to acquire or take control of Greenland, citing its strategic location and natural resources.His comments triggered strong opposition in Greenland, Denmark and other European countries and raised concerns about the impact on the NATO alliance.The standoff intensified in early 2026 before negotiations between Washington, Copenhagen and Nuuk eventually shifted toward a security agreement rather than a transfer of sovereignty.The final pact therefore gives Washington a substantially expanded military role without granting the United States ownership of Greenland.NATO welcomed the agreement, saying it would help advance security, stability and cooperation in the Arctic and North Atlantic.For Denmark and Greenland, the agreement provides a framework for closer US military cooperation while preserving the kingdom's sovereignty and Greenland's right to determine its future.Read: Trump Signs 'Tremendous' Greenland Security DealClick here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News
news.summary: Where will the US build its new Greenland military bases? Here's what to know about the locations, security deal and Greenland's sovereignty.

news.title: Asia stocks ride tech wave higher, oil stays subdued
news.text:
SYDNEY: Asian shares were aiming for a sixth session of gains on Wednesday as signs of consumer demand for AI apps continued to buoy ​tech stocks, while oil prices faltered on reports of increased supply out of the Middle East.

Sources told Reuters Saudi Arabia had ‌restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and may have already resumed exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

US President Donald Trump also claimed talks with Iran in New York had made progress, but then threatened to “annihilate” the country if a deal was not done.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addresses the UN General Assembly later on Wednesday and markets ​are alive to reports he might hold talks with Trump.

Brent futures eased 0.1% to $99.18 a barrel, while US crude fell 0.4% to $90.14 ​a barrel.

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington later in the day amid speculation a trade truce between the ⁠two countries will be extended, and there could be cooperation over AI.

Renewed buzz over AI helped South Korean stocks gain 1.2%, with Samsung and ​SK Hynix both up over 2%. Taiwan firmed 0.9%, to near all-time peaks.

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan added 0.7%, having now risen ​for six straight days. Chinese blue chips were little changed.

Japanese markets were closed for a holiday, but Nikkei futures were trading at 66,745 , almost 2,000 points above where the cash Nikkei closed on Friday.

“We expect a strong reopening in Japan tomorrow, with another move lower in crude, calm conditions in rates and Treasuries, and the Nasdaq cash and ​futures markets printing all-time highs,” said Chris Weston, head of research at broker Pepperstone.

“Memory stocks have taken the leadership baton, backed by another strong ​session for semi’s, which have recorded a sixth consecutive day of gains.”

Consumers fall for AI agents

The data hardware sector has been buoyed by strong consumer take up of ‌Meta’ Muse agent, ⁠which has topped US app download charts in the past two weeks.

Analysts are now keen to see how a similar product from Google Labs known as CC will fare with consumers.

On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures were both holding steady. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures and DAX futures added 0.3%, while FTSE futures gained 0.2%.

The dip in oil helped Treasury futures nudge higher, keeping 10-year yields below the 5.0% pain barrier.

However, two-year yields ​had again hit their highest since ​mid-2024 at 4.7879% as investors ⁠priced in the risk of more tightening from the Federal Reserve.

Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin and Boston Fed President Susan Collins on Tuesday both voiced support for last week’s rise in interest rates given concerns about inflation.

Futures markets imply a ​54% chance the Fed will hike again in October and have 33 basis points of tightening priced in ​by year end.

The ⁠prospect of higher rates helped the dollar eke out multi-week highs on the euro, sterling and Canadian dollar, improving its technical background. The euro was left pinned at $1.1440 and near a two-month low.

Analysts noted a call from Trump to ban U.S. diesel exports, was potentially bad news for European inflation since the zone relied ⁠heavily on ​U.S. shipments of the fuel.

Europe already faces a shortage of natural gas that could push ​energy prices higher into the winter.

The dollar was a shade firmer on the yen at 157.60 , with speculators wary of drawing more Japanese intervention on any push past 160.00.

In commodity markets, ​gold eased 0.3% to $4,341 an ounce , while copper neared record highs having climbed 18% so far this year.

news.title: Trump's attack on Kaitlan Collins backfires as CNN and MS NOW use it for lawsuit
news.text:
President Donald Trump's own words are being used against him as CNN and MS NOW boost their lawsuit against his White House media ban.

On Tuesday, several developments came in regarding CNN and MS NOW's lawsuit against Trump, even as the White House had yet to file its response before a deadline set for the end of the day.

Among the developments was CNN and MS NOW's lawyers adding to the court record Trump's attack against CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins at the United Nations earlier in the day.

Trump told Collins, "You shouldn't be here," because of the White House ban on CNN last week. Collins explained in the moment that she was let in by the United Nations.

MeidasTouch Capitol Hill correspondent Scott MacFarlane reported in a post on X that lawyers for CNN and MS NOW were submitting the statement as an exhibit to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, ahead of a court hearing on Wednesday.

Lawyers for the banned media outlets didn't finish there. Fallon Gallagher, a legal affairs reporter for MS NOW, reported via a post on X that lawyers for CNN and MS NOW, who are also representing Politico, informed Kelly of a D.C. Circuit Court ruling that "held the East Steps of the U.S. Capitol are a 'nonpublic forum' -- much like the White House -- and therefore any press restrictions must be 'viewpoint neutral.'"

The D.C. Circuit Court ruling about the East Steps came from a Trump appointee, who wrote the majority opinion, and was backed by an appointee of George H.W. Bush.

According to Gallagher, "the lawyers are using this ruling as additional evidence in support of the TRO ahead of tomorrow's hearing," referring to the temporary restraining order they're seeking to block the ban.

Meanwhile, Kellie Meyer, the White House correspondent for NewsNation, reported that the White House had no primary TV pool listed for Wednesday, but the secondary TV pool is led by Lindell TV, the outlet of MyPillow founder Mike Lindell, an election denier who lost the Republican primary for Minnesota governor.

news.title: Dollar holds near 2-month high as markets weigh rate hikes, Iran diplomacy
news.text:
SINGAPORE: The dollar steadied near its strongest level in two months on Wednesday ​on prospects of interest rate hikes in the near term, while easing oil prices on hopes for a diplomatic ‌breakthrough to end the Middle East war kept investors on edge.

The euro was at $1.1446 in early trading, loitering near its weakest level since late July. Sterling bought $1.3337. The dollar index , which measures the US currency against six rivals, was at 100.56.

The recent barrage of rate hikes and ​hawkish rhetoric from major central banks has taken centre stage in currency markets as the US-Israeli conflict with Iran ​drives oil prices higher and fans inflation worries.

Investors are now anticipating further tightening from central ⁠banks, with Federal Reserve officials flagging the possibility of more hikes if inflation does not ease.

“The dollar’s support from ​rates looks durable, but futures already price more tightening than the Fed’s own projections, so the dollar now needs the data ​to confirm it,” said Kieran Williams, head of Asia FX at Intouch Capital Markets.

Oil markets remain in the spotlight with Brent crude futures at $99.22 per barrel on hopes that diplomacy at the UN General Assembly could pave the way for a resolution to the Middle East war. Brent ​has risen 37% since the conflict erupted at the end of February.

US President Donald Trump warned that he could ​annihilate Iran if there is no deal to end the war, but also suggested an agreement could come soon amid the diplomatic efforts at the ‌UN.

“The ⁠good news is that oil prices have moderated somewhat from the highs but the path forward remains unclear given the lack of clarity around a possible resolution of the conflict,” said Michael Wan, a currency analyst at MUFG.

Investors are also waiting for a high-stakes meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping as the two leaders seek stability in a relationship ​under pressure over wide-ranging issues.

The Japanese ​yen was at 157.55 ⁠per US dollar as traders remain wary of the threat of intervention as markets judged the Bank of Japan’s rate hike to a 31-year high last week as insufficiently hawkish.

Two dissenting ​votes and the absence of a clear hawkish signal were enough to fuel doubts over how ​quickly the BOJ ⁠will tighten policy, particularly after the Fed raised rates last week and flagged further hikes ahead.

Japanese markets are closed for a holiday and the low liquidity period is seen by analysts as an optimal time for authorities to intervene if needed.

“The BOJ hike didn’t narrow ⁠the (yield) gap ​because the Fed hiked by the same amount two days earlier, so ​the lean is still higher,” said Intouch’s Williams.

“160 (per US dollar) remains the risk, but officials have reportedly moved away from telegraphing intervention and from any ​fixed level, so the cap could come earlier and in other forms.”

news.title: Kaitlan Collins Embarrasses Trump by Exposing Brutal Truth
news.text:
Kaitlan Collins has exposed the embarrassing reality for President Donald Trump after he lashed out at her at the United Nations.

The 80-year-old president, who has banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House, melted down at Collins, 34, after she asked him a question at the U.N.’s New York headquarters on Tuesday. 

But Collins set the record straight during an appearance on Anderson Cooper 360° Tuesday evening, saying, “The president himself there was saying something that CNN has never asserted about not covering him. We’ve never said that.”

“The president is the one who’s trying to dictate how we cover him,” she pointed out. “And of course, it is still our job to do so.”

Collins added the embarrassing detail that even members of Trump’s inner circle appear to be skeptical that his press ban will survive a legal challenge brought by the three outlets and set to be heard by a Trump-appointed judge Tuesday afternoon.

“There seems to be a reality inside the administration that this ban is not going to have legal muster and legal standing when it comes to a judge evaluating it tomorrow, and that likely things will return to the way they were before the president announced this on Friday,” she told Cooper. 

On Trump’s U.N. meltdown, Collins added that CNN had been credentialed by the United Nations. 

While Trump has prevented three outlets from entering the White House grounds by revoking their hard passes, he cannot stop them from covering him at a public gathering, no matter how much he dislikes them.

Collins argued that Trump’s visit to the U.N. headquarters underscores how his press ban is backfiring, pointing out that even as he met with a host of world leaders, the five major networks did not air his remarks.

NBC, ABC, CBS, and even the normally Trump-friendly Fox News have suspended White House pool duties and are refusing to assign reporting crews to cover Trump in protest of his ban. 

“So it is affecting the coverage of the president and the way that he likes to see it, which is broadcast on television, and in these key moments where he’s speaking with world leaders and answering questions from reporters,” Collins said. 

Collins then shifted the focus to Trump’s war with Iran, highlighting a new CNN poll that found approval of his handling of the conflict has fallen to a new low of 26 percent.

“They don’t approve of the way the president is handling it. They’re not approving of the way he‘s handling foreign conflicts overall,” she said. 

The CNN star later drove home the point that Trump barred CNN from covering him—not the other way around—on her own show, The Source, where she interviewed New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker. 

During his interview, Booker told Collins, “The way the president disrespected you should outrage all Americans,” and pointed out that media outlets across the political spectrum are standing together against Trump. 

“In a war against the First Amendment and the press, consider this a unifying thing for our country in defending CNN and, frankly, the kind of treatment that you endured today,” he said. 

Collins replied, “Well, obviously, we do appreciate the solidarity from our colleagues because I think the point that we’ve made during this is that if it can happen to CNN, it can happen to any other outlet.”
news.summary:
Reuters, CNNKaitlan Collins has exposed the embarrassing reality for President Donald Trump after he lashed out at her at the United Nations.

The 80-year-old president, who has banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House, melted down at Collins, 34, after she asked him a question at the U.N.’s New York headquarters on Tuesday. 

“I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” the president snapped. “You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me. You shouldn’t be covering me.”

news.title: Oil falls on increased Gulf supply and hopes for US-Iran talks
news.text:
PERTH: Oil prices drifted lower on Wednesday as Saudi Arabia began restoring crude supply on a ​critical pipeline to the Red Sea and on hopes for a diplomatic solution to the US-Iran ‌war through talks at the UN in New York.

Brent crude futures fell 7 cents, or 0.07%, to $99.18 a barrel as of 0119 GMT while West Texas Intermediate futures fell 35 cents, or 0.39%, to $90.17 per barrel.

While US President Donald Trump warned on ​Tuesday that he could “annihilate” Iran, he also said his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had held productive ​talks with mediators of Iran to end the war.

“I think there’s a lot of ⁠momentum for them to make a deal,” Trump said.

Optimism around improved supply and a push to end the ​nearly seven-month conflict drove benchmark Brent down to close below $100 a barrel on Tuesday for the first time since ​September 8.

“The market is currently feeling more constructive about the global oil supply picture than it was a few weeks ago,” said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade.

“The meeting of US and Iranian delegations in New York has given traders a ​glimmer of hope … Despite the continued tough rhetoric, including threats of ‘annihilation,’ the market is choosing to price in ​the possibility of talks.”

On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia restarted operations on its East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea, three sources briefed on the ‌matter said, ⁠with signs of an increase in Middle Eastern oil flows.

Drone attacks, which Saudi Arabia has blamed on Iraqi militia, forced the kingdom to shut the pipeline on September 11, halting crude loadings at the kingdom’s Yanbu port.

Since the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted oil flows from Saudi Arabia and its Gulf neighbours through the Strait ​of Hormuz, Riyadh has been ​using the pipeline to ⁠reroute around 4 million barrels per day — around 4% of global supply — to Yanbu.

Iraq, too, is increasing oil exports, its oil minister, Basim Mohammed, said on Tuesday.

The ​country is exporting more than 3 million bpd, he said, and expects to boost exports ​via Turkey ⁠to more than 600,000 bpd.

Provisional data from shiptracking firms Vortexa and Kpler pegged Iraqi crude exports in August at 2.3 million and 2.17 million bpd, respectively, up from July’s level but below February’s pre-war level of 3.7 million and 3.362 ⁠million bpd.

Adding ​to downward pressure on oil prices, industry data showed US crude inventories ​rose by 1.8 million barrels in the week to September 18, while analysts polled by Reuters had expected a decline.

Official weekly inventory figures from ​the US Energy Information Administration are due at 10:30 a.m. ET (1430 GMT).

news.title: Saudi king denounces Houthis in rare rebuke
news.text:
Rebels accuse Riyadh of deadly strikes as thousands flee• 154 people reportedly killed in fighting over past two days• G7 calls on Yemeni group to halt military actions, attacks on shipping• UK commits air-to-air refuelling support for Saudis

SANAA: The king of Saudi Arabia denounced Yemen’s Houthis as a “terrorist militia” in a rare statement on Tue-sday reacting to an attack that authorities said targeted the holy city of Makkah last week.

King Salman, 90, praised the armed forces and security services for defending the country, and condemned the recent Houthi attempt “to target Makkah”, calling it “a provocation to Muslims aro-u-nd the world”, according to the official Saudi news agency.

Houthis also accused Saudi Arabia on Tuesday of launching a wave of deadly strikes that killed civilians and prison inmates, as Riyadh seeks to repel an offensive that has seen the Iran-backed group seize strategic territory.

The recent Houthi takeover of Yemen’s Red Sea coast has left hundreds dead and heightened fears over global trade and shipping through the vital Bab al-Mandab strait.

It has also forced thousands to flee, with the United Nations on Tuesday forecasting the number of displaced could swell from over 130,000 today to more than 230,000 in the coming months.

The gains made by the Houthis have cemented the hold of Iran and its regional allies over two key waterways in the Middle East — and the straits of Bab al-Mandab and Hormuz — which are major shipping arteries for global flows of energy.

Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has sought to contain the Houthi advance with air strikes.

The Houthis have retaliated with attacks on Saudi territory, including a strike targeting the capital Riyadh for the first time in years.

The strike came days after Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of targeting the holy city of Makkah, though the fighters denied the claim.

In Yemen, the Houthis said a strike on a prison killed nine detainees, while they also accused the Saudis of killing six civilians including two children in the port city of Mocha.

Two more civilians were killed by strikes in Yemen’s Al-Jawf province, the Houthis added.

“A mother and child were killed, while her husband and two of her other children were wounded in strikes carried out by the Saudi enemy” in the Al-Batin area, Houthi media said, citing the Houthi health ministry.

‘Humiliation’

As violence has escalated, thousands of families have been forced from their homes, many for a second or third time.

“I hope I can find a house to live in with my children. We are exhausted by the heat, the dust and the humiliation,” Arwa, a mother of four children, told AFP at a camp for displaced people near Aden.

Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has in the past two days killed 154 people, military sources from both sides told AFP.

“The death toll from Saudi air strikes, clashes and artillery fire in the governorates of Taiz, Al-Jawf, Marib and Saada stands at 118,” Houthi military sources said, while government sources reported 36 killed in their ranks.

Saudi Arabia’s civil defence age-n--cy on Tuesday issued a warning of potential danger in the country’s sou-th near the Yemen border, the first alert since the Houthis launched their attack on Riyadh over the weekend.

The alert, which asked people to remain indoors and avoid open areas, was lifted a short while later.

UK, French support

G7 leaders representing Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States called on the Houthis to “immediately cease all military actions”.

They also demanded the Houthis end “all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith”, while urging Tehran “to end its arming of and support for the Houthis”.

Britain has also agreed to provide some military support to Saudi Arabia, defence minister Luke Pollard said.

A British tanker plane will provide “defensive” air-to-air refuelling for Saudi warplanes to help the country defend against Houthi strikes, the UK government confirmed late Monday.

“We’re doing it for national security reasons in support of our own national security,” Pollard told Sky News.

“In dangerous times, good friends stand together,” he added, insisting the support would be in compliance with international humanitarian law.

France also pledged to help secure Saudi energy infrastructure, a diplomatic source said. But “this in no way involves taking part in the conflict with the Houthis”, the French source said.

The Houthis have carried out attacks against facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.

Yemen’s government and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Sal-man have reportedly requested help from US President Donald Trump in fighting the Houthis.

More displacement feared

Renewed fighting in Yemen could see the number of refugees fleeing across the Red Sea to Djibouti jump to 10,000, while displacement inside Yemen could swell to over 230,000, the UN warned on Tuesday.

More than 100,000 civilians have been uprooted inside Yemen while others have risked dangerous sea crossings to flee the violence.

“Intensifying fighting in Yemen could drive more mass displacement,” United Nations refugee agency spokesman Babar Baloch told reporters.

news.title: Anthropic Launches Opus 5.5 After CEO Calls for Slower AI Development
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta – Anthropic on Tuesday launched Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in its new Claude 5.5 family and its first major model release since CEO Dario Amodei called for the pace of frontier AI development to be slowed.Anthropic said Opus 5.5 delivers performance comparable to Claude Fable 5.1 on most tasks while costing 40 percent less to run than its predecessor, Claude Opus 5, according to Yahoo Finance report.The new model is priced at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, compared with $5 and $25, respectively, for Opus 5. Anthropic said cache reads, which account for a large share of costs in agentic and coding workloads, will cost $0.20 per million tokens.Tokens are units used by AI models to process text, generally representing words or parts of words.Opus 5.5 Focuses on Performance and EfficiencyAnthropic said Opus 5.5 is its strongest Opus model to date, with improvements in coding, computer use and other complex professional tasks.The company said the model generates responses more than 30 percent faster than Opus 5 and requires less computing power to serve. Anthropic also said typical workloads will cost about 40 percent less than with the previous model.The company said early testers reported significant gains in complex work. In one test, Opus 5.5 completed a 680,000-line code migration in less than a day, while another test found it succeeded in improving the loading speed of a web application in 39 out of 40 attempts.Opus 5.5 is available through Anthropic’s Claude platform and API, as well as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry.Anthropic Highlights AI Safety MeasuresThe launch comes as the AI industry faces growing concerns about the potential risks posed by increasingly capable systems.Anthropic said Opus 5.5 underwent extensive alignment testing and external evaluations before its release. The company said it also includes safeguards for high-risk areas such as cybersecurity and biology.According to Anthropic, Opus 5.5 performed better than its previous models in its automated behavioral audit, which tests AI systems across thousands of simulated scenarios. The company also said the model is more resistant to prompt-injection attacks and less likely to take actions outside its assigned boundaries.Anthropic said it is continuing to improve its alignment research and develop new safety-training scenarios.Launch Follows Amodei’s Call to Pace AI DevelopmentThe release is notable because it follows Amodei’s recent call for a more measured pace of frontier AI development.Amodei argued that AI progress should be paced so that safety practices can stay ahead of increasingly capable models. Anthropic said the approach is intended to address potential risks while allowing society to benefit from AI advances, particularly in areas such as biology and medicine.The debate has intensified within the AI industry.Earlier this month, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation and criticized AI companies over what he described as inadequate attention to safety. Anthropic alignment science lead Evan Hubinger subsequently said he agreed with Coxon’s concerns and estimated that there was a greater than 10 percent chance advanced AI could cause human extinction.Amodei later published his argument for slowing the pace of frontier AI development.OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have expressed agreement with aspects of Amodei’s position, while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed back against predictions that AI could destroy humanity, saying such concerns are not grounded in science.US President Donald Trump has also dismissed some warnings about AI as conspiracy theories.Anthropic Plans More Claude 5.5 ModelsAnthropic said Opus 5.5 is the first release in its Claude 5.5 family.The company plans to release Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 in the coming weeks, with the models expected to bring similar improvements in performance, efficiency and safety.The launch underscores the challenge facing AI companies as they compete to develop more capable systems while addressing concerns over safety, security and the cost of running increasingly powerful models.Read: Researcher Awarded $6,500 for Breaching OpenAI Using ClaudeClick here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News
news.summary: Anthropic launches Opus 5.5, its first model since CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower pace of frontier AI development.

news.title: Six key talking points from Andy Burnham's UN speech as PM declares 'count on us'
news.text: In his inaugural speech to the UN, Andy Burnham championed Britain's role in global politics for the years ahead - assuring world leaders they can 'count on us'. In a comprehensive address, the new Prime Minister launched a scathing critique of Russia , unveiled a fresh international security pact with the US mere hours after meeting Donald Trump , reiterated calls for a two-state resolution in the Middle East, and introduced two significant domestic policies. The summit in New York marked Burnham's first major trial as an international diplomat since assuming the role of Prime Minister in July. Over the past few hours, he has held meetings with numerous world leaders for the first time, including Donald Trump, and used his 21-minute speech to outline his vision for British diplomatic leadership. Here are the six key takeaways from Andy Burnham's maiden speech to the UN. Once Burnham took to the podium and briefly touched upon Brexit, it swiftly became apparent who the antagonist of his speech would be: Russia. He proceeded to launch a fierce attack on Kremlin interference in British affairs, all while Putin's delegation looked on. The PM stated: "Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fear. "They've used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles. Forged the branding of 28 British organisations - including universities and the BBC. They've amplified far-right narratives. "And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 General Election." He further stated that Putin's government spends '£1.3 billion' on 'manipulating information'. "We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events," Burnham went on. "The idea that anyone would try to use such things to their advantage is just repulsive - but it is what they do." Russia has previously faced allegations of using unlawfully obtained documents about UK-US trade talks in an attempt to sway the 2019 election. Alarmingly, the Russian delegation displayed little emotion when Burnham levelled these accusations at them. Switching from his assault on Russia, Burnham unveiled one of two new domestic policies highlighted in his speech. He is setting up a new National Centre for Information Defence tasked with combating online falsehoods and deepfakes that harm British interests. The new unit will initially be led from the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet, with the new centre collaborating with intelligence agencies, government departments, the police and social media companies. After highlighting the 'insidious campaign' orchestrated by the Kremlin, Burnham said the new unit will be necessary as 'AI will multiply the threat' already posed by malicious actors online. The new government is poised to reveal a fresh decade-long strategy for the nation later this year, Burnham disclosed for the first time at the UN. It will concentrate on getting more people into employment - particularly young people - and alleviating the cost-of-living squeeze for most people, Burnham said, though he stopped short of announcing any specific policies at the time. Nevertheless, it seems Burnham is presenting this new strategy as an answer to insecurity. He declared 'security starts in every home', and he maintains that getting more people into employment makes them less vulnerable to being deceived by misinformation online. He said: "Part of the challenge is to lift our people up and create the opportunities they need. When inequalities grow too wide, our societies are at greater risk. "So we will work to make life more affordable for people. That will be at the heart of a new 10 year plan for Britain that we will bring forward later in the year." Just hours after his inaugural meeting with Donald Trump, Burnham unveiled a fresh national security agreement with the US as part of a portion of his speech which addressed AI concerns. He told delegates: "I am announcing today that we are developing a new AI defence partnership with the United States to protect our critical national infrastructure." Specifics of the agreement remain under wraps. Burnham continued to say that, as 'AI will also be a source of disruption to the way we live and work', he wants the UK to act as an 'honest broker' to establish 'a single set of global principles and standards' for the development of pioneering AI. As his speech began to wind down, Burnham shifted his focus to the Middle East, and reiterated calls for a two-state solution in Gaza. He denounced Hamas' 2023 attack on Israel as 'utterly horrific', but then said of Israel's response in the years since: "Far too many people have died, including so many children. Far too little aid is getting in, and it has gone on for far too long." That was why the UK 'prohibited trading goods with illegal settlements, acknowledged the Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territory is unlawful, and sanctioned those participating in the construction of illegal settlements' earlier this month, he said. But Burnham looked ahead and stated the two-state solution must 'remain viable'. He added: "We want to see the suffering and death finally come to an end. We want to see Israeli and Palestinian people living side by side in peace and security. And we will do all we can to keep the hope of that possibility alive." Burnham's initial move was to tell the world 'Britain is back' - and after 20 minutes, he clarified that meant global politicians can 'count on us' in the coming years. He wrapped up his address by stating: "You can count on us to stand up for those long standing British values of fairness and justice. "Count on us to fight racism, discrimination and the abuse of power wherever we see it. Count on us to bring people together. "Count on us to meet fear and division with unity and hope."
news.summary: Andy Burnham declared 'Britain is back' in his first UN speech as PM, accusing Russian agencies of disinformation and saying the UK is developing an AI defence partnership with the US.

news.title: The appeal of putting your name on something
news.text:
Melvin Durai

US President Donald Trump recently issued an executive order instructing US federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario, which sits between America and Canada, as “Lake America.” He did this following a trade dispute with Canada, his way of antagonising Canadians. They should be relieved, however, that he did not try to rename Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes of North America, as “Lake Trump.” Trump, after all, loves putting his name on anything and everything. Well, perhaps not everything. I’m sure he wouldn’t be thrilled to see the “Donald J. Trump Waste Disposal Center.” Most people want to be remembered after they’re gone — and one way to achieve this is to leave your name on a building.

All you need to do is fi nd a prominent building and visit it in the middle of the night with a ladder and a can of paint. If you do a good job, the people who live or work in the building may assume that you did something special to have the building named after you. Wealthy people can easily get their names on buildings, just by owning a building themselves or donating money to an organization that owns a building. Universities are full of buildings and many of them carry the names of their benefactors. For example, Anuradha and Vikas Sinha recently donated 20 million dollars to the University of North Texas (UNT) to establish the Anuradha and Vikas Sinha College of Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Analytics. It may seem egotistical to require a building to be named after you in order to make a large donation, but it’s a good way for institutions and organizations to raise money.

Not everyone expects their name to be promoted — many people donate money without expecting anything in return. But if someone wants to give me 20 million dollars, I’ll be happy to name everything I own after them: my house, my car, even my dog. Making a large donation isn’t the only way to get your name on a building. If you do something great, perhaps reaching the top of your field, there’s a chance that you’ll be honoured with a naming of some sort. It might be a building, but it could also be an airport, a park or a road. Mahatma Gandhi’s name appears on countless universities, schools, buildings and streets. He didn’t have to make a large donation. All he had to do was free India. While there’s no shortage of people who’d love to see their names on buildings, perhaps only a handful in the entire world can match the unabashed desire of Trump to see his name on as many edifices as possible. His business ventures have given him a dozen Trump Towers around the world, including in Kolkata, Mumbai and Pune, as well as several other apartment buildings and hotels that carry his name. In New York City alone, there’s the Trump Building, Trump Palace Condominiums, Trump Parc and Trump Parc East, Trump Park Avenue and Trump World Tower.

More than a dozen golf courses around the world are also named after him. Is Trump satisfied with this? No, he wants to put his name on many more buildings, even buildings that are already named for other people. He is adamant about having the John F. Kennedy Centre for the Performing Arts in Washington D.C. be renamed the Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Perhaps one day he’ll even ask UNT to do a renaming, enrolling students in the Donald J. Trump and Anuradha and Vikas Sinha College of Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Analytics.

news.title: END OF PAX AMERICANA
news.text:
Pedro Abramovay & Julia Sakr-Tierney

From the moment it was announced, the ceasefire between the United States, Israel, and Iran has been marked by a different form of confrontation: peace on the precipice of war and war on the brink of resolution. The memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June was supposed to kick off 60 days of negotiations, culminating in a comprehensive peace. Instead, it has been followed by continued fighting, including US and Iranian strikes on the Strait of Hormuz and the seizure of Yemen’s Red Sea coast by the Houthis, which threatens to disrupt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb. Tens of thousands of air strikes have failed to force Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran says it will lift the siege in exchange for an end to four decades of sanctions.

The US is doing the opposite: maximising already maximal sanctions. But Iran is no closer to capitulation, underscoring America’s inability to manage the aftermath of its own fury. Across the region, force is looking less like strength than instability. In Gaza, war is not a means of securing a political objective; it is the objective. With the Gaza Doctrine of disproportionate force and destruction, Israel is waging war not only on Hamas, but on the international legal order itself. Israel has also deployed that doctrine in southern Lebanon, where airstrikes have continued uninterrupted, despite two ceasefires and a peace agreement that makes a farce of Lebanese sovereignty. It is often argued that, under US President Donald Trump, an unmasked might-makes-right approach has overtaken US foreign policy, exemplified by the extraordinary rendition of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and the war against Iran. The US has abandoned even the hypocritical tribute it once paid to international laws and institutions.

Whereas US President George W. Bush’s administration made its case for invading Iraq before the United Nations Security Council, Trump’s administration is acting on the basis of pure coercion, without any pretence of consultation (except in lockstep with Israel). But this amounts less to a rupture than an escalation. From extrajudicial executions by drones to indefinite detention at Guantánamo Bay, the US spent a generation systematically abrogating the post-war “rules-based” international order it once authored, not merely narrowing the rules’ universal premises but making them essentially disposable. The path to the Trump Doctrine of global dominance was paved by the previous administration’s complicity in the genocide in Gaza.

Nonetheless, the open embrace of coercive militarism has made a difference, though not the one Trump expected. Far from bolstering US dominance, this approach has eroded it. When the distinction between war and peace dissolves into a ceasefire that is neither, and months of bombardment fail to deliver anything like victory, force looks less like strength and more like pointless destruction. Perpetual war makes any world order impossible. The application of raw power will trigger resistance; war crimes will lead to international opprobrium. While coercion will render sovereignty conditional, it cannot ensure continued domination. The question, then, is what comes next. Coercive militarism has provoked a period of profound instability. But its failure could usher in more balanced relations among states: a new multilateralism grounded in sovereignty and reinforced by regional and global mechanisms that promote universal rights, mutual restraint, and collective decision-making regarding shared resources, norms, and values. Such a multilateralism is undoubtedly aspirational. But every country, including the US, has an interest in building it.

The UN would not be irrelevant in this new system. But with the UN issuing only one resolution on the Iran war (criticizing Iranian retaliation but not the US-Israeli attacks that instigated it) diplomacy needs different defenders. Regional initiatives are particularly important, and their promise is already becoming apparent. Consider the US-Iran MoU. The negotiations were mediated by an unlikely coalition led by Pakistan and Qatar with support from Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey. This represents a major shift from negotiations for the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), the nuclear deal Iran concluded with the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, Germany, and the European Union. The difference is all the more notable, given that in 2010, the countries that would go on to sign the JCPOA swiftly dismissed a nuclear-fuel swap that Brazil and Turkey negotiated with Iran. As then-Brazilian Foreign Minister Amorim lamented, “traditional centers of power [would] not share gladly their privileged status.”

Another example is the informal consultative framework among Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey aimed at building a more stable regional security architecture shaped by shared norms, including a commitment to forsake the use of force. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey have also formalized a mutual defence agreement, known as the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, that does not identify an adversary and leaves open the possibility of others joining. While its significance is being tested by the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the broader trend is undeniable: the emergence of a more pluralistic regional order, in which countries take more responsibility for their own security, rather than allowing the US to impose its will.

Like the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait is now effectively closed, owing to the asymmetrical force unleashed in response to US escalation. What we are witnessing in the Middle East is not only extreme violence, but also extreme overreach. But the war that is catalysing the disintegration of a US-led multilateral order is also opening space for a more sustainable multilateralism rooted in rights, restraint, dignity, diplomacy, and respect for sovereignty.

news.title: Pakistan stands out amid flurry of diplomacy at UNGA
news.text:
As Islamabad presses Washington and Tehran to return to talks, Trump reveals ‘three-hour meeting’ with Iranian delegation• US president hails PM Shehbaz as ‘terrific man’; diplomatic efforts win praise from UN chief• Dar joins counterparts from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Egypt in stressing need to uphold Islamabad MoU

NEW YORK: Pakistan remained front and centre on Tuesday, amid a flurry of diplomatic activity at UN Headquarters, as world leaders came together to address the 81st General Assembly session.

Both PM Shehbaz Sharif and Deputy PM Ishaq Dar spent a busy day filled with whirlwind meetings, engaging with leaders from around the world, as they continued to push for a diplomatic solution to the US-Iran war, which has taken a toll on global trade and energy markets.

Although he is scheduled to address the UNGA tomorrow (Thursday), PM Shehbaz was mentioned by US President Donald Trump in his speech, who called him a “terrific man”.

“The prime minister of Pakistan — terrific man — said that Donald Trump was responsible for saving 30 million lives and probably many more than that,” he said as he rattled off a list of conflicts that he claimed to have helped settle: Pakistan-India, Thailand-Cambodia, Armenia-Azerbaijan, and the Gaza conflict, among others.

Pakistan has been vigorously pursuing diplomacy to help bring the United States and Iran back to the negotiating table, even as uncertainty clouded a possible meeting between Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the UNGA.

Those efforts seem to have borne fruit when, after sending mixed signals during his UNGA speech, President Trump said that his team had met an Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the General Assembly.

“It was a meeting that lasted for three hours; it ended an hour ago,” Trump told reporters after a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelensky. “It was a very good meeting. I can’t imagine why they wouldn’t want to do it; it’s greatness or obliteration.”

He added that the meeting was “productive” and that “They have another one scheduled in the very near future”.

According to diplomatic sources at the United Nations, Pakistan has been “quietly but persistently urging” both Washington and Tehran to maintain indirect contacts and “remain positively open” to direct talks.

A day earlier, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had travelled to Tehran and met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni, with the mediation process among the issues discussed.

During the visit, Iranian officials expressed appreciation for Pakistan’s continuing efforts to promote regional peace and stability.

The diplomatic efforts were also appreciated by Secretary-General António Guterres, whose spokesperson said a day earlier that the outgoing UN chief was “very grateful and appreciative” of the efforts by Pakistan’s leadership to mediate between Washington and Tehran and help end the violence.

Guterres’ spokesman Stéphane Dujarric told a news briefing in New York that Pakistan’s role was “critical”, and described the understanding reached in Islamabad as “a great achievement.”

He said Guterres had remained in close touch with the Pakistani leadership as part of efforts to achieve the shared objective of ending the conflict.

Asked about the efforts of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Pakistan’s army chief to mediate between Iran and the United States, Dujarric said the UN chief appreciated the Pakistani leadership’s efforts to bring an end to the violence.

“Other countries have also been involved,” he said, “but I think Pakistan’s role has been critical.”

Dujarric also endorsed renewed direct engagement between Washington and Tehran, saying the UN “always” supports dialogue.

“Diplomacy is our middle name, so to speak,” he said, adding that any re-engagement between the United States and Iran, as they had previously pursued, could help bring an end to the conflict, which he said was “hurting a lot of people.”

Iranian President Pezeshkian is expected to address the UN General Assembly today (Wednesday) and hold bilateral meetings with world leaders.

Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that no meeting with Iranian representatives was currently scheduled, but that Washington was open to such talks if they had the prospect of producing a positive result.

Iran, meanwhile, has signalled that its delegation in New York has authority to pursue diplomacy. Tehran has also conveyed proposals to Washington through mediators, keeping open the possibility of a return to negotiations.

Sideline meetings

On Tuesday, Deputy PM Dar participated in a key ministerial meeting of the Regional-4 (R-4) group, where he was joined by the foreign ministers of Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt.

The R-4 group has been focused on regional security and emerged in March amid efforts for mediation between the US and Iran.

As the group met in New York, DPM Dar reaffirmed “Pakistan’s strong commitment to the R-4 framework and expressed the need for continued engagement for enhancing regional peace and prosperity”, the Foreign Office (FO) said in a statement.

It added that the participants exchanged views on the latest situation in the region and expressed full support for efforts aimed at a peaceful resolution of the situation.

A statement issued by the Permanent Mission of Pakistan to the UN said that the ministers’ consultative meeting on Sept 21 on the sidelines of the session also discussed recent regional and international developments.

“The ministers underscored that dialogue and diplomacy remain the only path towards sustainable resolution, and in this context they underscored the need for upholding the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding for lasting peace and stability,” the statement said.

Meanwhile, PM Shehbaz met with several world leaders, including President of Somalia Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, Kenyan President William Ruto, and Kuwaiti crown prince Sheikh Sabah Khaled Al-Hamad Al-Sabah.

news.title: Trump Backs India-Middle East-Europe Corridor, Calls For Energy Routes To Bypass Iran
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has backed the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), saying the ongoing conflict in the region has highlighted the need for alternative routes to transport energy without relying on infrastructure linked to Iran.
Addressing a gathering of Gulf Cooperation Council and Arab leaders on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said attacks targeting commercial shipping had demonstrated the risks facing existing energy networks in the Middle East. "...Iran's terrorist attacks on commercial shipping in neighboring countries have shown the need to shift Middle East energy infrastructure away from the Iranian checkpoints. That's why my administration strongly supports the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor and other places in the form of getting oil out, whether it's pipelines or anything else," Trump said.
Trump Backs IMEC
Trump's endorsement comes as the conflict has disrupted established shipping and energy routes in the region. He said the situation had made it increasingly important to develop infrastructure capable of moving energy through alternative pathways.
The US president also presented the current moment as an opportunity for wider regional cooperation, arguing that long-standing challenges could be addressed through closer coordination among countries in the region. "Together, we're on the verge of overcoming challenges that have plagued this region for decades..." he said.
Advancing efforts for a safer, more prosperous Middle East. The Gulf Cooperation Council meets in New York City. 🤝 pic.twitter.com/wInPPW1Nrh
— The White House (@WhiteHouse) September 22, 2026
ALSO READ: ‘I Stopped India-Pakistan War’: Trump Repeats Claim At UNGA, Says Shehbaz Thanked Him
Trump also described the leaders attending the gathering as important partners in Washington's efforts to pursue greater stability and economic prosperity across the Middle East. He said, "It is an honor to be here with some of America's greatest and closest friends, allies, and partners to continue our effort toward a safer and more prosperous Middle East."
Hormuz Disruption
The push for alternative energy routes comes amid disruption to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important passages for oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.
The conflict, which began after US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, has led to a significant decline in vessel movement through the waterway. The disruption has prompted Gulf oil producers and international buyers to explore alternative options for transporting energy.
Around 20 million barrels of oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz each day in 2025. The waterway also handled nearly one-fifth of global LNG trade, making it a critical link in international energy supply chains.
Any prolonged disruption to the route can therefore affect the movement of energy and create wider implications for global markets and prices.
ALSO READ: National Herald Case: Sonia-Rahul File Reply In Delhi HC, Oppose ED’s Plea
How IMEC Works
IMEC was unveiled during the 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi as a major connectivity initiative linking India, the Middle East and Europe.
The proposed corridor consists of two principal routes. The Eastern Corridor is planned to connect Indian ports, including Mundra and Kandla, with major Gulf ports such as Fujairah and Jebel Ali.
From the Gulf, the Northern Corridor would run across Saudi Arabia and Jordan before reaching Israel's Haifa Port. From there, the network is intended to connect with European destinations, including Piraeus and Marseille.
The broader project envisages a combination of maritime shipping routes, rail and road connectivity, as well as energy and digital infrastructure.

news.title: Republican Backs Diesel Export Ban in Red State That Saw $26 Gas Price
news.text: Alaska Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is calling for a temporary halt to U.S. diesel exports as fuel prices surge, weeks after gasoline in one of the state’s remote villages soared to over $26 a gallon. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he backs the idea, as the administration examines whether a temporary restriction would be feasible. Sullivan proposed a moratorium until the conflict in Iran ends and energy exports resume flowing through the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that keeping more American diesel at home could help rebuild reserves ahead of winter and lower costs. “American fuel should stay home with Americans,” he said in a statement Tuesday. “The cost of diesel is just too damn high.” Diesel hit a record $6.53 per gallon average Tuesday nationwide, according to AAA, and was $6.67 in Alaska. The national average has risen nearly 31 cents over the past week, according to GasBuddy. “Diesel rose in every state, with five states seeing increases exceeding 50 cents per gallon,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a statement. He added that continued strikes on Russian oil refineries are tightening global diesel supplies, while regional refinery issues are adding pressure in the Great Lakes. Any broader shift in diesel prices will depend heavily on overseas developments, with new Houthi attacks and fresh U.S.-Iran escalations leaving the outlook uncertain, De Haan said. On August 26, Newsweek reported that drivers in Shungnak, Alaska, were paying $26.82 per gallon. Financial expert Michael Ryan told Newsweek that the extreme price was driven in part by local transportation problems, with fuel having to be flown in after low water levels prevented barges from reaching the community. The village has faced unusually high fuel costs for years, with gas reaching $14 per gallon in 2022, according to the Alaska Beacon. When asked about Sullivan's proposal Tuesday, Trump said he had also called for a temporary halt to diesel exports. "I've called for that too. I've said, 'Let's not send out the diesel.' We make a lot of diesel," Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. "That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, it's sort of a flow. It's a balance." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who was seated near Trump, said the administration was considering whether an export restriction would be feasible. “We’re examining that—whether it’s feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work.” Trump and Bessent indicated the administration would move quickly in deciding whether to impose a restriction. The American Petroleum Institute (API) said Tuesday that restricting U.S. diesel exports would worsen refining challenges and further sting consumers. “Americans are hurting from rising diesel costs driven by an unprecedented disruption to global refining capacity,” API President and CEO Mike Sommers said. “We understand the administration is looking at every option to deliver relief, but restricting U.S. energy exports would only compound the problem.” Sommers added that the answer is “more supply and more flexibility,” rather than new restrictions. API said Gulf Coast refineries produce more diesel than the region consumes, making exports an important outlet for maintaining high refinery production. The group said limiting exports could force refiners to cut production of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel, tightening supplies even more. Several other Republicans have expressed support for the proposal this week. Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican from Iowa running for U.S. Senate, late Tuesday also called for a pause in diesel exports. “The House should return to DC immediately to work to pause diesel exports, suspend the gas tax, fully unleash E15 and biodiesel, and work on a diesel relief program for truckers and farmers,” she wrote on X. Senator Chuck Grassley, another Iowa Republican, has also called for a temporary diesel export embargo. “I encourage President Trump to put a temporary embargo on diesel exports through executive actions,” he said on the Senate floor Tuesday. “It will help family farmers who feed and fuel the world.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune has said an export ban “probably” makes more sense as a way to address high diesel prices, though reopening the Strait of Hormuz would be the “best thing.” Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers is also calling for a temporary embargo on U.S. diesel exports, saying the war in Iran needs to end to bring costs down. “Here’s what we can do now: place a temporary embargo on Diesel exports. American energy should provide relief to American families first,” he wrote on X Monday. The push comes as disruptions to global energy supplies linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran have pressed oil and fuel markets. The Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil shipments, has faced severe disruptions since the conflict began, contributing to higher global energy prices. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins.
news.summary: Trump backed the proposal Tuesday as his administration weighs a full or partial restriction on diesel exports.

news.title: Trump’s White House media ban faces long odds in court, legal experts say
news.text: NEW YORK - U.S. President Donald Trump’s move to ban several news outlets from the White House over his dislike of their coverage likely runs afoul of U.S. legal prohibitions against viewpoint discrimination by the government, according to four legal experts.Trump’s announcement on Friday that he would ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico for reporting what he deemed “FAKE NEWS” was the latest move by his administration to curtail press access, part of the Republican president’s wider pressure campaign against news coverage he dislikes. Trump said on Saturday that he might ban other outlets as well.The president’s justification for the ban could be its undoing in a legal challenge because U.S. courts have long held that the government cannot condition press access on favorable coverage once it has opened a space to the media, according to legal experts.

news.title: World leaders seek to restore trust, transform UN at 81st session
news.text:
NEW YORK, USA – Word leaders at the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly raised critical issues that threaten the effectiveness of United Nations under the theme: “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.”

His Majesty King Mswati III who takes the floor on Wednesday, was amongst the throngs of world leaders who attended the 81st Session of the United Nations otherwise known as UNGA.

Outgoing UN Secretary General Antonio Gutteres delivered a wide-ranging speech that framed the world most pressing crisis as not just isolated problems, but different expressions of the same underlying struggle over how power is exercised and by whom.

Gutteres said the greatest power is not the power to dominate, when delivering his report, he said it is the power to build a future that works for everyone.

The UN SG described the past decade of his reign as of eroding international norms – from civilians targeted in war, and humanitarian workers killed, to international law “cast aside” and fraying trust between nations.

He said power itself is being fundamentally reshaped in three ways: Emergence of new State powers; Significant transfer of authority from governments to private corporations and individuals and the growing role of AI and autonomous weapons in decisions once reserved for humans.

“The faultlines in our world are widening,” he said. “Cracks have become canyons.”

Gutteres said rather than accepting fragmentation as inevitable, he called for galvanizing cooperation and a truly global network built on interdependence and shared rules while warning against sliding into rival blocs with separate economic and security systems, a scenario he has termed in recent years the Great Fracture.

Meanwhile, the Emir of Qatar Tarim bin Hamad Al Thani said the current crisis in the Gulf should come as no surprise to anyone. 

“It is the cumulative result of years of postponing crisis management through temporary solutions and unrealistic policies,” he said of the war between the US and Iran which has sprawled to impact a series of Gulf states. 

“At the heart of the dangerous situation we are witnessing lies an absence of a regional system of collective security. One that respects the sovereignty, security and territorial integrity of states. One that promotes the peaceful settlement of disputes and the non-interference in the internal affairs of states,” Al Thani said.

He said Qatar had recently called “from this very podium” for such a system and was now reiterating the appeal “after recent events have demonstrated the urgent need for it.”

Iran has sometimes been accused of strucking targets in neighboring Gulf countries with close ties to the US. 

Al Thani said that the restrictions on passage through the Strait of Hormuz amounted to the “lifelines of the global economy” being turned into bargaining chips, “with people on every continent bearing the cost, despite being far removed from the causes of the conflict.” 

The 46-year-old head of state said this was driving up prices not just for fuel but also for core other goods like food and medicine. 

United States President Donald Trump said America will never allow Iran, whom he described as the bully of the Gulf states to own a nuclear weapons.

“They were the, but they are the bully no more,” Trump said, adding that he had given Tehran numerous opportunities to drop its nuclear program and stop its support of militant groups across the regions.

“They refused, which was a big mistake.”

The US leader mentioned both the September 11 attacks and the October 7 attacks in Israel, the latter being carried out by Iran-backed Palestinian militant group Hamas.

“Just imagine such a vile regime was able to carry out terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield,” Trump said.

Trump concluded by saying he was facing a choice of whether to allow Iran regrow or to “annihilate” it. 

“Freedom was not a gift that Americans won easily after 250 years,” he said. “And it is not one that we will ever, ever surrender.”

He went on to tell of George Washington ordering the Declaration of Independence to be read to his troops in New York in 1776 as a British fleet approached the shore. 

Trump said that the first Americans “knew that it was not enough merely to believe in great principles, we must also have the will and the courage and the strength to defend them.” 

He said this was the challenge “for every nation in this room,” saying they should “go forward strong against the enemies of all humanity” and “refuse to shrink from” their duties to their people.

news.title: US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
news.text:
US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'

The US has criticised Australia's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms, saying it amounts to "censorship of protected speech".

Under Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, tech firms risk hefty fines if they fail to give users the option to turn off algorithms in a bid to protect them from harmful content.

In a rare submission to the proposed laws, the US embassy in Canberra said it had "serious concerns" and allowing the government to "enforce vague definitions of 'harm'" would lead to "viewpoint-based censorship".

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the legislation was not about giving governments control but giving it back to individuals.

"We ask that Australia clarify how exactly 'harm' and 'risks' shall be determined... ensuring these definitions do not encroach on protected speech," the US said in its submission.

The US also claimed that the proposed laws may risk "reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics" if tech firms had to "pre-emptively demote" them. 

An opt-out option would "allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements" on tech firms and this could affect users outside of Australia, it said.

"Mandated platform design features, especially when applied to algorithms, may affect what users see, say, and hear not just in or from Australia, but globally."

The US also called on Australia to address industry concerns that the "biases and preferences" of government officials do not "disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech".

Another worry was that the proposed laws could affect Australia's "reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation," the submission said.

The criticism comes during Albanese's visit to the US to speak at the UN's General Assembly about his government's tech policies.

On Tuesday, local time in New York, Albanese responded to the criticism and claims of the proposed laws being government overreach.

"It's not about giving government control," he told the media in New York.

"It's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices."

US President Donald Trump meanwhile used his speech at the UN to play down fears about AI, rejecting proposals for guardrails on it and arguing it should be renamed "super intelligence" as "the use of the word artificial makes it sound fake".

This latest move by Australia to protect its online users from harm comes less than a year after the country introduced a social media ban for children under 16 last December.
